name: Sif's golden hair: the prank that starts the wager
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The trickster prank that triggers the making of the six great treasures, told in Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 43). T1: SIF is the wife of THOR the thunder-god, and she is famous in Asgard for her long, thick GOLDEN HAIR that reaches to the ground; poets say it is more beautiful than any hair the gods have seen. T2: LOKI the trickster, for no reason but mischief, sneaks up on Sif while she is sleeping and SHEARS HER HEAD BALD with a knife. T3: when Thor discovers what has been done to his wife's hair, he seizes Loki and threatens to BREAK EVERY BONE IN HIS BODY unless Loki goes down to the dwarves and gets Sif hair of REAL GOLD that will grow on her head like living hair. T4: Loki hurries down to SVARTALFHEIM (the dark-elves' underworld home) and goes to the workshop of the SONS OF IVALDI, three dwarf-brothers who are the master smiths of that world. They spin out for him a fall of hair from PURE GOLD, fine as any real hair, that will fasten to Sif's scalp and grow like her own -- and while they are at it they also make TWO more marvellous gifts (the folding ship SKIDBLADNIR and the spear GUNGNIR, saved for their own rungs). T5: Loki flies back to Asgard with the three treasures, and the moment the golden hair touches Sif's head it takes ROOT and begins to grow -- Thor is appeased, Sif is glorious again, and the whole disaster is patched. But Loki cannot resist stopping on the way to BOAST that the Sons of Ivaldi are the finest smiths in all the worlds -- and the boast is what starts the wager with the brothers Brokkr and Sindri that will end with Loki's mouth sewn shut. Further rungs: Snorri gives Sif no origin-story other than being Thor's wife and the mother of Ullr the skier and the archer; the golden-hair myth is one of the clearest survivals of Sif as a grain-goddess (blonde standing corn); the phrase 'Sif's hair' becomes a kenning in the skaldic poets for GOLD itself.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (the whole 'Gifts of the Gods' passage -- Loki cutting Sif's hair, Thor's threat, the Sons of Ivaldi in Svartalfheim, the three treasures, the golden hair rooting on Sif's head). Skaldic corroboration: the kenning 'Sif's hair' for gold in Egill Skallagrimsson and elsewhere (Skaldskaparmal 42, list of gold-kennings). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sif' and 'Sons of Ivaldi' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Sif', 'Sons of Ivaldi', 'Skaldskaparmal' -- Loki cutting Sif's hair as prank, Thor's ultimatum, Ivaldi's sons making the replacement in Svartalfheim, the hair rooting on her head, the same visit also producing Skidbladnir and Gungnir, Sif's hair as gold-kenning. framing_note: The OPENING ladder of the six-treasures cycle -- everything downstream (Mjolnir, Gungnir, Draupnir, Skidbladnir, Gullinbursti, Brokkr sewing Loki's mouth) begins with THIS prank. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Thor threatens to break EVERY BONE in Loki's body until Loki fixes it) and T5 (the moment the golden hair touches her scalp it takes ROOT and grows). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Loki cut off Sif's hair' AND ask what Loki did; describe the SCENE (Thor's wife asleep, a trickster with a knife, a bald head at dawn) and let the recall be WHOSE hair, WHO did it, or what Thor demands. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Greek stories of Zeus's punishments or the Christian stories of divine anger cornering a wrongdoer -- a god's rage cornering a trickster. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Loki tricks (Sleipnir's siring, the wall-builder), other Aesir wives (Frigg, Freyja, Idunn -- adjacent-real), other dwarf-smith trios (Brokkr and Sindri who come NEXT, the Nibelung dwarves in the Volsung cycle). Wrong smiths: it is the Sons of IVALDI who make the hair, not Brokkr and Sindri (they are the second wager).
history_overlap: None with history (this is pure myth from Snorri's Prose Edda). GEOGRAPHY owns nothing here -- Svartalfheim is a mythic world, not a real place. ANIMAL bank might mention Thor's goats, but the goats are not part of this story.

name: The wager: Loki bets his head with Brokkr and Sindri
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The bet that produces Mjolnir and costs Loki his lips, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 43). T1: on his way back from getting Sif's golden hair (and Skidbladnir and Gungnir) from the Sons of Ivaldi, LOKI stops in the dwarf-quarter of SVARTALFHEIM and cannot resist BOASTING that the Sons of Ivaldi are the finest smiths in all the nine worlds. T2: this boast reaches the ears of two brothers, the dwarves BROKKR and SINDRI (Snorri also calls Sindri by the name EITRI). Brokkr, insulted for his brother's craft, tells Loki that his brother Sindri can make THREE TREASURES finer than Ivaldi's -- and Loki, who never turns down a bet, wagers HIS OWN HEAD on it. T3: the two brothers get to work in their forge. Sindri is the one at the anvil doing the actual smithing; BROKKR'S JOB is to work the BELLOWS without stopping, because if the bellows falter for a single moment the metal will spoil. Loki, realising he might actually lose his head, changes shape into a BITING FLY and attacks Brokkr to break his rhythm. T4: on the first treasure (Gullinbursti the golden boar) the fly bites Brokkr's HAND -- Brokkr keeps pumping. On the second (Draupnir the ring) it bites his NECK -- he keeps pumping. On the third (Mjolnir the hammer) the fly bites his EYELID so hard that BLOOD runs down into his eye and he has to raise a hand for one instant to wipe it -- and in that instant the hammer comes out with a HANDLE TOO SHORT to grip in two hands. T5: the two dwarves take all six treasures (three from Ivaldi, three from themselves) up to Asgard and lay them before ODIN, THOR and FREYR as judges. The gods examine the golden hair, Skidbladnir, Gungnir, Gullinbursti, Draupnir and Mjolnir in turn -- and judge MJOLNIR the finest of all six, short handle and all, because it is the best weapon the gods have ever been given against the giants. Brokkr and Sindri have won the wager, and Loki has lost his head. Further rungs: Snorri names Sindri as the smith and Brokkr as the bellows-worker, though the hammer is often called 'Sindri's work' in the poets; the fly-form (fluga) is Loki's stock shape-change alongside mare and salmon and old woman; the short handle is why Thor needs iron gauntlets and a girdle of might (Megingjord) to wield Mjolnir at full force.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (the whole wager sequence -- Loki's boast, Brokkr's counter-boast, the head-wager, Sindri at the anvil and Brokkr at the bellows, Loki as the biting fly, the three bites on hand/neck/eyelid, the short handle on Mjolnir, the gods' judgement in favour of Mjolnir). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Greek stories of gods bargaining with mortals (Apollo and Marsyas's flute-contest) or the Christian stories of high-stakes wagers (Jesus fasting for forty days) -- a bet where the cost is a body-part. Wrong bribers: Loki does not offer them gold, he bets his HEAD.

name: Mjolnir: the hammer with the too-short handle
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Thor's hammer, greatest of the six treasures, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 43 for its making, Gylfaginning 21 for its properties). T1: MJOLNIR (Old Norse 'mjollnir', 'crusher' or 'grinder') is the war-hammer of THOR the thunder-god; it is the greatest weapon in Asgard and the gods' best defence against the giants of Jotunheim. T2: it was forged in the dwarves' underworld by SINDRI at the anvil and his brother BROKKR at the bellows, as the third and finest of their three treasures in the wager against Loki (see prior ladder). Its shaft came out TOO SHORT to hold in two hands because Loki, as a biting fly, bit Brokkr's eyelid until blood ran down and Brokkr had to raise a hand to wipe it (Skaldskaparmal 43). T3: Snorri lists its powers in Skaldskaparmal 43 -- it will never miss its target when thrown; it will always RETURN to Thor's hand no matter how far he hurls it; and it can be shrunk down small enough to hide inside Thor's SHIRT. T4: to WIELD the hammer at full force Thor needs two other pieces of gear: iron gauntlets called JARNGREIPR to catch the returning hammer without burning his hands, and a belt of might called MEGINGJORD that doubles his already-godlike strength (Gylfaginning 21). T5: Thor's hammer is used to CONSECRATE weddings and funerals (small hammer-shaped amulets have been dug up all over Viking-age Scandinavia), and at RAGNAROK Mjolnir kills JORMUNGANDR the world-serpent -- and Thor, choked by the serpent's venom, walks nine steps and falls dead, hammer still in his hand. In the meantime the hammer is stolen by the giant Thrym and Thor has to dress in a wedding veil to get it back (that story runs on its own ladder). Further rungs: hammer-pendants in Viking graves worn as counter-charms to the Christian cross during the conversion period; the name Mjolnir comes from a Norse root related to 'meal' as in ground grain (a hammer that grinds); Thor's hammer at weddings is what Loki mocks in Lokasenna, saying Thor's hammer 'blessed the bride' whom Loki claims to have slept with.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (Mjolnir's making by Sindri/Brokkr, the short handle from Loki's fly-bite, its never-missing return-to-hand and shrinking properties, the gods judging it the finest of the six treasures); Gylfaginning 21 (Thor's three treasures: hammer, iron gauntlets Jarngreipr, belt Megingjord); Gylfaginning 51 (Mjolnir killing Jormungandr at Ragnarok, Thor walking nine steps and falling). name: Gungnir: Odin's spear that never misses
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Odin's signature weapon, one of the two great gifts of the Sons of Ivaldi, from Snorri's Prose Edda. T1: GUNGNIR is the SPEAR of ODIN the All-Father, chief of the Aesir and lord of the slain. T2: it was forged by the SONS OF IVALDI -- the same dwarf-brothers who made Sif's replacement golden hair -- during Loki's first errand down into Svartalfheim (Skaldskaparmal 43). It was one of the three treasures Loki brought back before Brokkr and Sindri made their three, and it was one of the six laid before the gods for judging. T3: Gungnir will NEVER MISS its target once thrown, no matter what stands between spear and victim. Snorri says of it in Skaldskaparmal 43 that it 'never stops in its thrust' -- once launched it goes clean through anything to strike its mark. T4: Odin uses Gungnir in one of the founding acts of the Norse cosmos: at the Aesir-Vanir war he throws GUNGNIR OVER THE HEADS of the enemy host as a formal declaration that they are dedicated to him and doomed (Voluspa 24, and echoed in the Ynglinga saga). Warriors after him imitate the gesture -- hurling a spear over an enemy army to consecrate them as sacrifices to Odin. Sacred oaths in Norse tradition are also sworn on Gungnir's point, because a promise sworn on it cannot be broken without doom. T5: at RAGNAROK Odin rides out with Gungnir at the head of the einherjar (the chosen dead) from Valhalla to face FENRIR the great wolf -- and for all Gungnir's never-missing perfection Odin is SWALLOWED whole by Fenrir (Gylfaginning 51). Odin's son Vidar then avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart with a special shoe. Further rungs: Gungnir's runes are said to be carved down its shaft, empowering it (Sigrdrifumal 17); the Aesir-Vanir war spear-throwing is the mythic origin of the Viking-age battle custom of consecrating the enemy to Odin before battle; the Ynglinga saga has Odin himself, when dying of old age, cut himself with a spear-point to 'be given to Odin' -- ritual self-dedication using Gungnir's shape.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (Gungnir among the treasures of the Sons of Ivaldi; its never-missing property); Poetic Edda, Voluspa 24 (Odin throwing his spear over the host at the Aesir-Vanir war); Sigrdrifumal 17 (runes on the spear-point); Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 9 (Odin's spear-consecration practice; Odin's self-wounding with the spear at his death). name: Skidbladnir: the ship that folds into a pocket
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The magic folding ship of Freyr, the second gift of the Sons of Ivaldi. T1: SKIDBLADNIR (Old Norse 'skidbladnir', 'assembled from thin pieces of wood') is a ship belonging to FREYR the god of harvest and sunshine, one of the Vanir who lives among the Aesir. It is the greatest ship ever made. T2: it was forged by the SONS OF IVALDI during Loki's first errand for Sif's hair, and given to Freyr as their second treasure (Skaldskaparmal 43). Snorri says of it that it is 'the best of all ships and the most skillfully made'. T3: Skidbladnir is BIG ENOUGH to carry ALL of the AESIR in full armour with their weapons and their horses; and yet, T4: when the voyage is done it can be FOLDED UP LIKE A CLOTH and put into a POUCH small enough to slip into a pocket (Skaldskaparmal 43, Gylfaginning 43). T5: it has one further trick -- as SOON as its sail is raised Skidbladnir catches a FAIR WIND straight to wherever Freyr wants to sail, so it needs no rowing and cannot be becalmed. Grimnismal 43 in the Poetic Edda gives all three properties in one stanza: 'Skidbladnir, the best of ships is built for shining Freyr; but of ships is Naglfar the greatest, which Muspell's people own' -- naming Skidbladnir alongside its dark counterpart Naglfar, the ship built of dead men's nails that carries the giants to Ragnarok. Further rungs: Skidbladnir has one of the neatest 'infinite-inventory' shapes in world mythology -- fits an army but folds to a handkerchief; Naglfar the doom-ship of Ragnarok is Skidbladnir's exact opposite (grows longer every time a dead person's nails go uncut, hence the Norse custom of trimming a corpse's nails before burial); Freyr's other treasures are the golden boar Gullinbursti (see its own ladder) and the sword-that-fights-by-itself which he later gives away to woo the giantess Gerd -- for which loss he pays at Ragnarok.

name: Draupnir: Odin's ring that drips eight more every ninth night
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Odin's self-multiplying gold-ring, second of Brokkr and Sindri's three treasures. T1: DRAUPNIR (Old Norse 'draupnir', 'the dripper') is a GOLD ARM-RING or torc that belongs to ODIN the All-Father. T2: it was forged by the dwarf brothers SINDRI (at the anvil) and BROKKR (at the bellows) during their wager against Loki, as the second of their three treasures -- Loki as a biting fly bit Brokkr's NECK while they made it, but Brokkr kept pumping (Skaldskaparmal 43). T3: its magic property: every NINTH NIGHT, eight NEW gold rings of equal weight DRIP from Draupnir onto the arm that wears it -- so an owner of Draupnir grows richer in gold by eight rings every nine nights forever. T4: in the great tragedy of BALDR the beloved son of Odin, Odin lays DRAUPNIR on his son's funeral pyre when Baldr is burned aboard his ship Hringhorni (Gylfaginning 49) -- the ring goes down with Baldr into Hel. Later, when the god Hermod rides down to Hel to try to bargain for Baldr's return, Baldr gives him DRAUPNIR to carry back up to Odin as a token that Hermod really has seen him (Gylfaginning 49). T5: even later Skirnir uses Draupnir as one of the bribes he offers to the giantess GERD when he goes wooing on Freyr's behalf, promising her the ring that drops eight of itself every nine nights (Skirnismal 21); Gerd refuses gold in the end and yields for a different reason. So Draupnir passes through three of the great Norse story-cycles -- the wager, Baldr's death, and the wooing of Gerd. Further rungs: 'the dripper of Draupnir' becomes a skaldic kenning for GOLD itself; the ninth-night cycle echoes other Norse ninths (Odin hangs on Yggdrasil nine nights; Ragnarok's herald-blast is Heimdall's ninth blast); the ring shows up in Old English echoes in Beowulf's 'ring-giving' as the archetype of the good lord who parts with treasure to his men.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (Draupnir among the three Brokkr/Sindri treasures, dripping eight rings every ninth night); Gylfaginning 49 (Draupnir laid on Baldr's pyre, sent back up by Baldr with Hermod as token); Poetic Edda, Skirnismal 21 (Skirnir offering Draupnir to Gerd). name: Gullinbursti: the golden boar that lights its own way
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Freyr's golden boar, the first of Brokkr and Sindri's three treasures, from Snorri's Prose Edda. T1: GULLINBURSTI (Old Norse 'gullin-bursti', 'gold-bristled') is a mechanical BOAR of pure GOLD, given to FREYR the sun-and-harvest god as one of the six great treasures. It is also called SLIDRUGTANNI ('cutting-tusk'). T2: it was forged by SINDRI at the anvil and BROKKR at the bellows -- the FIRST of their three treasures made during the wager with Loki. Loki as a biting fly bit Brokkr's HAND while they made it, but Brokkr kept pumping the bellows (Skaldskaparmal 43). Sindri throws a PIGSKIN into the fire and pumps up the flames with Brokkr's bellows, and out steps the golden boar fully formed. T3: Gullinbursti has three marvellous properties -- it can RUN FASTER over land, sea, and air than any horse; it can carry Freyr across the sky and over the waves as easily as a boat over calm water; and, most famously, its GOLDEN BRISTLES SHINE SO BRIGHTLY that it LIGHTS UP THE NIGHT wherever it goes, so Freyr never rides in darkness (Skaldskaparmal 43). T4: Freyr rides Gullinbursti at BALDR'S FUNERAL, arriving with the golden boar drawing his chariot (Gylfaginning 49) -- the boar's light glows over the beach where the great ship Hringhorni is burning with Baldr aboard. T5: at RAGNAROK Freyr, weaponless because he long ago traded his self-fighting sword to Skirnir for the giantess Gerd, will fall to the fire-giant Surt -- but Gullinbursti still runs at the head of his chariot into that last battle. Further rungs: the boar-as-solar-image is one of the oldest Indo-European symbols (Celtic Twrch Trwyth, the Boar of Ben Bulben in the Irish Fianna cycle -- but those are BOAR-HUNT stories, not solar-boar stories); Freyr's other boar Hildisvini ('battle-swine') is ridden by his sister Freyja, but is a separate creature; the golden bristles as light-source is a Norse image later borrowed for chivalric romances of magical steeds.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (Gullinbursti's making from a pigskin thrown in the fire, its speed, its light-giving bristles, its being the first of Brokkr and Sindri's three); Gylfaginning 49 (Freyr arriving at Baldr's funeral drawn by Gullinbursti); Skaldskaparmal 17 (Freyr called 'god of Gullinbursti'). name: Loki's lips sewn shut: the head-forfeit dodged, the awl instead
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The punchline of the six-treasures wager, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 43). T1: at the end of the great smithing-contest, the gods judge MJOLNIR the finest of the six treasures, and BROKKR and SINDRI have won the wager. T2: the price agreed was Loki's HEAD -- Brokkr comes forward to claim it. Loki, cornered, tries every argument to escape: he offers Brokkr gold instead, but Brokkr refuses; he tries to run away, but Thor catches him. T3: at last Loki finds his loophole. He says to Brokkr, 'YOU MAY TAKE MY HEAD BUT YOU MAY NOT TOUCH MY NECK' -- because the wager was for a head, not a neck. Brokkr cannot cut off a head without cutting a neck, and the wording of the bet gives Loki the wriggle. T4: BROKKR, in fury at being cheated by lawyer-talk, decides on the next best thing -- if he cannot take Loki's head, he will at least SILENCE the mouth that spoke the boast that started the whole business. He asks for an AWL (a leather-worker's needle, whose name in Norse tradition is VARTARI) and, holding Loki still, tries to punch a hole through Loki's LIPS. T5: the awl will not go through Loki's skin. Snorri says Brokkr calls for his brother's SHARPER awl -- and that one punches straight through. Brokkr then SEWS LOKI'S LIPS SHUT with a leather thong called VARTARI, so the trickster cannot speak until he tears the stitches out again -- and Loki does tear them out, and the scars remain on his mouth. Further rungs: 'the mouth of Loki' becomes a skaldic phrase for a stitched-up lie; the loophole ('the head but not the neck') is one of the earliest surviving Indo-European trickster escape-clauses, echoed in the Greek stories of Odysseus and in medieval legal riddles; the awl called Vartari is the ONLY named awl in Norse literature; Loki's willingness to be sewn rather than beheaded is the last time he cooperates with any consequence -- from this point on his tricks turn darker (the killing of Baldr; the tying of Nari's entrails).
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skaldskaparmal 43 (the judgement in favour of Mjolnir, Loki's head-claim, the 'my neck was not in the bet' loophole, Brokkr calling for the awl, Sindri's sharper awl going through, the thong Vartari sewing the lips). name: Angrboda's children: Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Loki's three monstrous children by a giantess, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 34). T1: LOKI, though married to the goddess SIGYN, secretly takes as a lover the giantess ANGRBODA ('grief-bringer') who lives in JOTUNHEIM, land of the giants. By her he fathers THREE MONSTROUS CHILDREN. T2: the first is FENRIR, a wolf; the second is JORMUNGANDR, a serpent; the third is HEL, a girl who is HALF ALIVE AND HALF DEAD -- Snorri says one side of her face and body is the healthy pink of a living woman and the other side is BLACK AS A CORPSE (Gylfaginning 34). T3: Odin, seeing the three children in a prophecy as the doom of the gods at Ragnarok, orders them brought to Asgard. HEL he casts DOWN into NIFLHEIM, giving her rule over all who die of sickness or old age (not warriors, who go to Valhalla) -- and her hall is called ELJUDNIR ('sprayed with damp'), her dish HUNGER, her knife FAMINE, her bed SICK-BED, and her threshold STUMBLING-BLOCK. T4: JORMUNGANDR the serpent Odin THROWS INTO THE SEA that surrounds Midgard, the world of men -- and the serpent grows so long in that sea that it encircles the WHOLE WORLD and bites its own TAIL. So it is called the MIDGARD-SERPENT or the WORLD-SERPENT. T5: FENRIR the wolf Odin has RAISED IN ASGARD, thinking the gods can control him if they keep him close. But Fenrir grows faster and stronger than any wolf has grown, and only TYR the war-god is brave enough to go on feeding him. When the gods realise how huge he is becoming, they will have to trick him and bind him -- and Tyr will lose his hand (that ladder is next). At Ragnarok all three children fight the gods: Fenrir swallows Odin, Jormungandr and Thor kill each other in a single mutual blow, and Hel lets loose her dead. Further rungs: the mother's name Angrboda literally means 'she who brings grief' and is the earliest omen; Hel's whole household is a series of grim puns (Ganglati the servant 'slow-mover', Ganglot the maidservant 'slow-goer'); Jormungandr's biting-its-own-tail image (Ouroboros in Greek) is one of the oldest world-encircling-serpent motifs; Fenrir's brothers in some sources include the wolves SKOLL and HATI who chase the sun and moon.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 34 (Loki and Angrboda in Jotunheim, the three children Fenrir/Jormungandr/Hel, Hel half-living half-corpse, her hall Eljudnir with the named dishes and beds, Jormungandr thrown into the sea and encircling the world, Fenrir raised in Asgard); Voluspa 39-40 (Angrboda's brood at Ragnarok). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (three children: a wolf, a snake, and a HALF-LIVING-HALF-CORPSE girl) and T4 (Jormungandr is so long it wraps the whole world and bites its own tail). name: Gleipnir and Tyr's hand: the six impossible things
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The binding of Fenrir the wolf and the price it cost, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 34). T1: FENRIR the wolf, one of Loki's three monstrous children by Angrboda, grows so huge in Asgard that only TYR the war-god will go near him to feed him. The gods hold council and decide they must BIND FENRIR before he becomes strong enough to destroy them. T2: they try TWO chains first. LOEDING, an iron chain, Fenrir SNAPS with a single kick, thinking it a game. DROMI, a chain twice as strong, he also breaks. T3: the gods send a messenger down to SVARTALFHEIM to the DARK DWARVES, who make a fetter called GLEIPNIR ('the ensnarer'). It is thin and soft as silk, but made of SIX IMPOSSIBLE THINGS -- Snorri lists them in Gylfaginning 34: (1) the SOUND OF A CAT'S FOOTFALL, (2) the BEARD OF A WOMAN, (3) the ROOTS OF A MOUNTAIN, (4) the SINEWS OF A BEAR, (5) the BREATH OF A FISH, and (6) the SPITTLE OF A BIRD. This is why cats make no sound, women have no beards, mountains have no visible roots, and so on -- the dwarves used them all up in the fetter. T4: the gods take Fenrir out to the island of LYNGVI on the LAKE AMSVARTNIR and challenge him to test this thin ribbon. Fenrir SMELLS THE TRICK immediately and refuses -- unless one of the gods will lay a HAND IN HIS MOUTH as a pledge of good faith. Every god refuses. Then TYR, alone, walks up to Fenrir and lays his RIGHT HAND into the wolf's mouth. T5: the gods tie Gleipnir round Fenrir. Fenrir strains against it and it only grows tighter. Realising he has been cheated, he BITES OFF TYR'S HAND -- and Snorri says this is why Tyr from that day on is called ONE-HANDED, and why one hand is called 'the wolf's-joint' in old kennings (Gylfaginning 34). Fenrir is chained down with Gleipnir passed through a stone slab called GJOLL and anchored to a rock called THVITI, and a SWORD is set upright in his jaws to prop them open, and his slavering makes the river VON that flows out of his mouth -- until Ragnarok, when he breaks free. Further rungs: Tyr is the god the gods honour when they need a sacrifice made honestly -- he is the only Aesir willing to LOSE something for the group; his name gave the English day Tuesday ('Tyr's day'); Snorri's six-impossible-things list is one of the earliest surviving 'sky is blue because...' etiologies in Western myth.
source: PRIMARY: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 34 (the binding of Fenrir: chains Loeding and Dromi broken, dwarves making Gleipnir from six impossible ingredients, listing all six, Fenrir demanding a hand in his mouth, Tyr laying in his right hand, Fenrir biting it off, the fetter anchored through Gjoll to Thviti, the sword propping his jaws, the river Von); Voluspa 40-44 (Fenrir at Ragnarok breaking free). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Gleipnir' and 'Tyr' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Gleipnir', 'Fenrir', 'Tyr' -- Loeding and Dromi broken, Gleipnir from six impossibles named individually, Tyr's hand as pledge, hand bitten off, one-handed god. framing_note: The SACRIFICE-FOR-THE-GROUP ladder -- Tyr's hand is one of the best-known 'named cost' scenes in world myth. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the fetter is made of SIX impossible things -- a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle) and T5 (only TYR would put his HAND in the wolf's mouth, and he LOST it). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Norse binding-stories (Loki bound with Nari's entrails -- later ladder), other body-part costs (Odin trading his eye at Mimir's well -- separate ladder), other 'thin-thing that binds' magic objects. name: Sleipnir: Loki as a mare and Odin's eight-legged horse
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The story of the horse Odin rides and how it came to have eight legs, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 42). T1: SLEIPNIR is the horse of ODIN the All-Father -- greatest of all horses, GREY as storm-cloud, and famous for having EIGHT LEGS instead of four. T2: he was fathered on LOKI by the giant stallion SVADILFARI during the affair of the WALL-BUILDER of Asgard (see next ladder). T3: the wall-building giant came with SVADILFARI, a magic stallion that could HAUL BOULDERS THREE TIMES HIS OWN SIZE -- and the giant was going to finish Asgard's wall on time, meaning he would win Freyja, the sun and the moon. Loki (who had talked the gods into the bargain) was ordered to fix things or die. T4: LOKI TURNED HIMSELF INTO A BEAUTIFUL MARE and ran neighing past Svadilfari at the height of a night's work. The stallion snapped his traces and CHASED the mare into the woods, and the two spent the night together. The wall was not finished on time (giving Thor his opening to kill the builder), and MONTHS LATER Loki (still transformed, or in the form of a mare again) gave birth to SLEIPNIR the eight-legged foal (Gylfaginning 42). T5: Loki brought the strange colt to Odin, and Sleipnir became the greatest of horses -- so fast he can ride between the worlds, so sure-footed he carries Odin down into Hel itself. In Baldr's death-story it is Sleipnir that carries HERMOD down to Hel to bargain for Baldr's return (Gylfaginning 49). In the Poetic Edda's Sigrdrifumal 15 the runes are said to be carved on Sleipnir's teeth. Further rungs: eight legs are variously interpreted as (a) four pallbearers carrying a coffin (a shamanic death-horse figure), (b) speed doubled beyond ordinary horses, (c) an image of a horse mid-gallop with hooves in eight positions; Loki's mare-form is his most famous shape-change alongside fly, salmon and old-woman-Thokk; the eighth-century Tjangvide picture-stone from Gotland shows Odin riding an eight-legged horse into what appears to be Valhalla -- one of the earliest surviving images of the Sleipnir myth.

name: The Master Builder: the walls of Asgard for Freyja, the sun, and the moon
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The bargain that nearly cost the gods their sky and their goddess, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 42). T1: a stranger arrives at ASGARD offering to build the gods a WALL strong enough to keep out FROST-GIANTS and MOUNTAIN-GIANTS. The stranger will not name himself, and comes with only one horse. T2: he asks a shocking price -- if he finishes the wall in ONE WINTER, without help, the gods will give him FREYJA the goddess of love as his wife AND the SUN AND MOON out of the sky. If he fails he gets nothing. The gods think this impossible and are ready to refuse; LOKI persuades them to accept, but only if the builder does it all HIMSELF, without a single helper, in one winter and one day less. T3: the builder agrees on one condition -- he may use his HORSE. The gods agree. The horse's name is SVADILFARI, and Snorri says the stone-hauling Svadilfari does is TWICE the work the builder does himself (Gylfaginning 42). By THREE DAYS BEFORE SUMMER the wall is almost done -- only the gateway remains. T4: the gods, realising they are about to lose Freyja and the sun and the moon, TURN ON LOKI and threaten him with death unless he undoes it. LOKI TURNS HIMSELF INTO A MARE and runs neighing at Svadilfari at the height of a night's work; the stallion snaps his harness and CHASES the mare all night into the forest, and no stone is hauled that night. The wall is not finished on time. T5: the builder, seeing he has been cheated of his prize, FLIES INTO A GIANT-RAGE -- and reveals that he was a FROST-GIANT all along in disguise. THOR, who was away in the east fighting trolls, comes home just in time; he raises MJOLNIR and CRUSHES THE BUILDER'S SKULL, sending him 'down to Niflhel' (Gylfaginning 42). Later Loki (still transformed, or turned again) gives birth to SLEIPNIR, the eight-legged horse that becomes Odin's. Further rungs: this is one of the clearest examples of the gods HAPPILY breaking a sworn oath because the sworn party turns out to be a giant in disguise; the near-loss of the SUN and MOON to a giant is one of the recurrent Norse anxieties (also in Skoll and Hati chasing the sun and moon); the moral punchline in Snorri is that oaths sworn to giants are worth less than the safety of the sun and moon -- kids can see the dark trickery on both sides.

name: Lokasenna: the flyting at Aegir's feast
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Loki's insult-poem at the sea-god's banquet, from the Poetic Edda (Lokasenna). T1: the sea-giant AEGIR (also called Hler or Gymir) hosts a great FEAST in his hall under the sea, brewing ale in a vast cauldron he has borrowed from the giant Hymir. All the AESIR and VANIR come except Thor, who is away in the east fighting trolls. T2: LOKI arrives uninvited and immediately KILLS one of Aegir's servants (Fimafeng) in a fit of jealousy at the servant's praise. The gods drive him out. But Loki comes BACK, forces his way to the door, and demands his rightful seat and drink. T3: what follows is a FLYTING -- a formal insult-poem contest -- in which Loki, one by one, names EVERY GOD'S SHAME. He calls out Bragi for cowardice; Idunn for sleeping with her brother's killer; Gefjon for taking gold to sleep with a boy; Odin for cheating in war and for dressing as a woman; Frigg for sleeping with Odin's own brothers Vili and Ve while Odin was away; Freyja for having slept with every one of the Aesir including her own brother Freyr; Njord for being an Aesir hostage who was 'sent east as a target'; Tyr for having only one hand (thrown as insult, not compassion); Sif for having secretly slept with Loki himself. Every accusation stings because every one has just enough truth (or story-truth) in it that the god cannot cleanly deny it. T4: at last THOR arrives, back from his eastern trip, and Loki turns his tongue on Thor -- but Thor, unlike the others, does not answer with words. He raises MJOLNIR and threatens to smash Loki's head. Loki, having faced every argument in the world, folds instantly at the hammer's shadow. Snorri's later Prose Edda notes that after THIS Loki finally flees Asgard, and it is FROM this feast that the gods later hunt Loki down and bind him under the snake (that ladder is next). T5: the last stanzas name what will happen to Loki -- 'Long shall you be bound with your own son's guts' -- and Loki curses AEGIR that his hall will burn (which it does at Ragnarok). Further rungs: 'flyting' is a Germanic verse-duel form found in Old English (Beowulf's exchange with Unferth) and later Scots poetry -- Lokasenna is the great mythic exemplar; the poem's structure is one god at a time, one accusation, one defence, moving down the hall; Loki's specific choice to accuse Sif of sleeping with HIM connects the Lokasenna back to the golden-hair story (the OLD grudge is why Loki cut Sif's hair in the first place, some readers argue).

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Loki NAMED EVERY GOD'S SHAME one by one -- Odin dressing as a woman, Frigg with Odin's brothers, Freyja with her own brother) and T4 (Thor's answer to insults was NOT WORDS, it was RAISING MJOLNIR). Wrong ender: THOR with MJOLNIR, not Odin with a word.

name: Baldr's death: mistletoe, Hodr, and the giantess who would not weep
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The killing of the best-loved god, and why he could not be brought back, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 49). T1: BALDR the beloved son of ODIN and FRIGG is the fairest and gentlest of the Aesir, so bright that light shines from him. He begins to have DREAMS of his own death, and the gods are alarmed. T2: FRIGG his mother goes throughout the nine worlds and takes an OATH from every creature, every plant, every metal, every stone and every sickness NOT TO HARM her son. Every being in the world swears -- except one. Frigg passes over a plant so young and small she thinks it cannot matter: the MISTLETOE (Icelandic 'mistilteinn') growing on a great oak east of Valhalla. T3: because nothing else can harm him, the gods invent a NEW GAME at their assemblies -- they hurl stones and swords and spears at Baldr, and the weapons all bounce off. LOKI, in disguise as an old woman, visits Frigg and asks whether ANY thing at all was left un-sworn. Frigg carelessly mentions the young mistletoe. Loki goes and cuts a SPRIG of mistletoe and shapes it into a small dart or arrow. T4: at the next game Loki approaches HODR (Icelandic Hodr, sometimes Hoðr in old spellings), Baldr's blind brother, standing alone at the edge of the ring. Loki says, 'You should throw too -- I will guide your arm.' He puts the mistletoe dart into Hodr's hand and directs his aim. The dart flies -- and Baldr FALLS DEAD (Gylfaginning 49). The gods are struck silent; they cannot speak or act for grief. T5: Frigg begs a rider to go to HEL and ask for Baldr back. HERMOD rides Sleipnir DOWN into Hel and Hel-the-queen agrees on ONE condition -- that EVERY LIVING THING in all the worlds must WEEP for Baldr. Frigg and the gods send messengers to every corner. Every creature weeps -- until they find one giantess sitting alone in a cave, named THOKK ('thanks'), who refuses. 'Thokk will weep dry tears for Baldr's funeral,' she says, 'let Hel keep what she has' (Gylfaginning 49). Baldr stays in Hel; and Snorri says most people believe Thokk was LOKI IN DISGUISE. Further rungs: Baldr's ship-pyre HRINGHORNI is so heavy it takes the giantess Hyrrokkin (riding a wolf bridled with vipers) to launch it; Odin whispers into dead Baldr's ear on the pyre a word only he knows (Vafthrudnismal 54); Baldr will return AFTER Ragnarok, ruling the reborn world with Hodr -- reconciled, both innocent -- and this is one of the loveliest post-apocalypse promises in Norse myth.

name: Loki's punishment: bound with Nari's entrails, Sigyn with the bowl
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: Loki's final capture and the earthquake-making torment, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 50) and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna. T1: after LOKI's insults at Aegir's feast (Lokasenna) and his role in the killing of BALDR, the Aesir at last decide that Loki must be caught and PUNISHED. Loki flees and hides on a mountain, building himself a house with four doors so he can see danger from every direction. T2: Loki spends his days in the form of a SALMON in the waterfall of FRANANG, catching food. But he makes a mistake -- while sitting by the fire he begins IDLY MAKING THE FIRST FISHING-NET IN THE WORLD, weaving it from linen. The gods, catching up to him, see the pattern of a half-burnt net in his fire-ash and IMITATE IT -- and use that first net to CATCH LOKI at his own waterfall (Gylfaginning 50). Thor grabs the salmon by the tail -- which is why (Snorri says) all salmon are tapered at the tail. T3: the gods drag Loki to a cave. They take his TWO SONS by his Asgard wife SIGYN -- named NARI (or Narfi) and VALI (or in some versions Vali the god turns Vali the Loki-son into a wolf who kills his own brother). One brother is turned into a wolf and TEARS THE OTHER TO PIECES. The gods take the DEAD SON'S ENTRAILS and use them to BIND LOKI to THREE FLAT STONES -- one under his shoulders, one under his loins, one under his knees. The entrails HARDEN INTO IRON. T4: SKADI the giantess-goddess (whose father Thjazi Loki had helped kill in an earlier story) takes a great SNAKE and fastens it above Loki's face so that its VENOM DRIPS onto his forehead. T5: SIGYN Loki's wife, faithful even now, stands beside her bound husband holding a WOODEN BOWL above his face to CATCH THE DRIPPING VENOM. As long as Sigyn holds the bowl the venom does not touch Loki. But every time the BOWL FILLS she must turn away to empty it -- and in that instant the venom DRIPS on Loki's face, and he THRASHES so hard in his bonds that the whole earth SHAKES. Snorri says this is what causes EARTHQUAKES. Loki remains bound like this until RAGNAROK, when the bonds finally break and he sails with the dead to the last battle. Further rungs: the first fishing-net motif is a classic 'fatal invention' -- the trickster caught by his own new tool; the salmon-tail-shape etiology is one of Snorri's charming 'why animals look this way' asides; the mercy of Sigyn standing bowl-in-hand for centuries is one of the tenderest images in Norse myth, and one of the few times the poem shows a wife's devotion outlasting a husband's evil.

name: Kvasir and the Mead of Poetry: dwarves, blood, and honey
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: How poetry itself came to Asgard, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 5-6). T1: after the AESIR-VANIR war ended the two divine tribes SEALED THEIR PEACE by all SPITTING INTO A VAT together. From that spittle grew a MAN -- KVASIR, wisest of all beings, who could answer any question ever asked. T2: Kvasir travelled the worlds teaching. He came at last to the hall of TWO DWARVES named FJALAR and GALAR -- who INVITED HIM IN and then MURDERED HIM. They drained Kvasir's BLOOD into two vats called SON and BODN and a kettle called ODRERIR, mixed the blood with HONEY, and BREWED it into a MEAD (Skaldskaparmal 5). Anyone who drank of this Mead of Poetry became instantly a POET and a wise-man. T3: the two dwarves next INVITED the giant GILLING to visit; they killed him by drowning him at sea and then, when his wife wailed for grief, killed her too by dropping a millstone on her head from above the doorway. Gilling's son SUTTUNG came looking for revenge -- and forced the two dwarves out onto a tidal rock to drown. The dwarves BOUGHT their lives by giving Suttung the MEAD. Suttung took it home to his mountain HNITBJORG and set his daughter GUNNLOD to guard it in a deep chamber. T4: ODIN, hearing of the mead, disguised himself as a labourer under the name BOLVERK and travelled to the farm of Suttung's brother BAUGI, where he outworked nine slaves (killing them by tricking them into cutting each other with a whetstone he had sharpened). He demanded as payment help getting to the mead. Baugi bored a hole into Hnitbjorg with a drill called RATI -- and Odin turned into a SNAKE and slithered through. Inside he spent THREE NIGHTS with Gunnlod, and each night she gave him ONE SIP of the mead -- and in three sips he DRAINED ALL THREE VESSELS to the bottom. T5: Odin turned into an EAGLE and flew for Asgard with the mead in his crop. Suttung, seeing him escape, TURNED HIMSELF INTO AN EAGLE TOO and pursued. The gods in Asgard put out great VATS as they saw Odin approaching. Odin SPAT THE MEAD into the vats -- but in his hurry (with Suttung closing) he ACCIDENTALLY LOST some out the other end -- and that spilled portion, called 'the SHARE OF THE BAD POETS', is what any hack-versifier can pick up (Skaldskaparmal 6). Suttung the eagle burned to death in a fire the gods lit at the wall. And that is why poetry belongs to Asgard, and why sometimes even bad poets can find a few good lines. Further rungs: 'Kvasir's blood' is a skaldic kenning for POETRY itself; the two vessels Son ('reconciliation') and Bodn ('offering') and the kettle Odrerir ('inspirer') keep their names as kennings for verse; Odin's eagle-form here is the pair to his other shape-changes (serpent to enter, eagle to leave) and is one of the great heist-narratives of world myth.

name: Idunn's apples: Loki, the eagle, and the kidnapping
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: How Loki nearly cost the gods their immortality, from Snorri's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal 1-2). T1: IDUNN is the goddess who keeps the APPLES OF YOUTH in a box -- golden apples that the gods eat to STAY YOUNG. Without them the Aesir age like any mortals. Idunn is the wife of BRAGI the god of poetry. T2: Odin, Loki and Hoenir go wandering, kill an ox for supper, and cannot get the meat to cook. A great EAGLE speaks from a nearby oak and says the meat will cook only if he can have his share first. Loki gets angry and swings a pole at the eagle -- the pole STICKS to the eagle and Loki's hands stick to the pole, and the eagle SOARS off dragging Loki through rocks and bushes until Loki begs for mercy. T3: the eagle is really the giant THJAZI in disguise, and his price is IDUNN and her APPLES. Loki, to save himself, PROMISES. Back in Asgard he lures Idunn out of the walls, telling her he has found even MORE beautiful apples in a wood nearby and wants her to bring hers to compare. Thjazi as the eagle SWOOPS DOWN, snatches Idunn and her apple-box, and flies with her to his hall THRYMHEIM in Jotunheim. T4: without the apples the gods begin to AGE -- Bragi's beard turns grey, the goddesses wrinkle, Odin's shoulders bend. They meet in council and quickly work out that Loki was the last to see Idunn. They threaten his life. Loki agrees to fix it. He borrows FREYJA'S FALCON-CLOAK, flies to Thrymheim, finds Idunn alone (Thjazi is off fishing), TURNS HER INTO A NUT in his talons, and flies back for Asgard. T5: Thjazi comes home, sees Idunn gone, takes eagle-form and PURSUES. Loki-as-falcon reaches Asgard's walls just ahead of the giant. The gods have built a great BONFIRE OF WOOD-SHAVINGS on top of the wall. Loki flies over and the shavings are LIT the instant Thjazi's eagle-shape passes -- Thjazi's wings CATCH FIRE, he falls INSIDE the walls of Asgard, and the gods KILL him. Idunn is restored to nut-shape-to-goddess and the apples come back. Thjazi's daughter SKADI comes armed to demand blood-price for her father, and gets to marry an Aesir god chosen by the sight of feet (she picks Njord thinking his beautiful feet are Baldr's). Further rungs: the apples are one of only a handful of Norse-specific 'food-of-immortality' motifs, parallel to Greek ambrosia; Idunn's turned-into-a-nut form (in Loki's talons) is one of the neatest 'small-and-hidden' rescue-transformations in myth; the daughter Skadi's arrival is the beginning of her own long story (see the strand-of-marriage-and-hunt).

name: Thor's wedding veil: recovering Mjolnir from Thrym
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The comic-heroic tale of Thor's disguise, from the Poetic Edda (Thrymskvida). T1: THOR wakes one morning to find MJOLNIR HIS HAMMER GONE. He shakes his beard in fury (Thrymskvida 1) and calls for LOKI. Loki borrows FREYJA'S FALCON-CLOAK and flies to Jotunheim to find out who has stolen the hammer. T2: he finds THRYM, king of the frost-giants, sitting on a burial-mound braiding gold collars for his hounds. Thrym cheerfully admits he took MJOLNIR and buried it EIGHT MILES DEEP under the earth (Thrymskvida 8), and says he will only give it back if the gods send him FREYJA as his BRIDE. T3: Loki brings the news home. FREYJA refuses with such violence that the great necklace BRISINGAMEN snaps around her neck. The gods hold an assembly at which HEIMDALL (Snorri's Prose Edda names Heimdall as speaker in some retellings; Thrymskvida has an unnamed speaker) has a plan -- dress THOR AS A BRIDE and send HIM to Jotunheim instead. Thor refuses at first, then agrees, terrified of losing Mjolnir. T4: they dress THOR in a BRIDAL VEIL, in Freyja's Brisingamen necklace, in a woman's KIRTLE, with a bunch of keys at his belt and clattering pendants at his breast (Thrymskvida 15-19). Loki comes along dressed as the maidservant. At the giants' wedding-feast Thor EATS an ox, EIGHT salmon, all the sweetmeats, and drinks THREE VATS OF MEAD alone. Thrym stares. Loki whispers in the giant's ear that the bride has been so eager for the wedding she hasn't eaten for eight nights. Thrym leans in for the wedding kiss, LIFTS THE VEIL, and staggers back from the LIGHTNING-EYES of Thor -- Loki says the bride hasn't slept for eight nights either. T5: as is the custom, Thrym calls for MJOLNIR to be brought and LAID ON THE BRIDE'S LAP to hallow the marriage. The moment the hammer touches Thor's knees, HE SEIZES IT AND KILLS every giant in the hall -- Thrym FIRST, then Thrym's sister who was demanding wedding-gifts, then every guest (Thrymskvida 30-32). Thor comes home with Mjolnir in hand. Further rungs: this is the most COMIC of the great Thor tales -- the thunder-god blushing in a veil, out-eating a whole giant hall, saving himself with Loki's quick lies about the bride's appetite; the phrase 'to hallow with the hammer' is Snorri's language for Mjolnir consecrating a wedding or funeral, and Thrym's mistake is thinking a giant wedding can be hallowed by the same gesture; Thrymskvida is one of the shortest and most beloved poems of the Poetic Edda.

name: Loki's brood in the Norse imagination: kinships and enmities
strand: Norse: Loki's tricks and the six great artifacts
scope: The map of Loki's family, showing how the trickster is tied to almost every Norse story-cycle, drawing on Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 33-34, 42, 50) and the Poetic Edda. T1: LOKI is not one of the Aesir by blood -- he is the son of two GIANTS, his father FARBAUTI ('cruel-striker', a name for lightning) and his mother LAUFEY ('leafy island') or NAL ('needle'). He was accepted into Asgard as ODIN'S SWORN BROTHER (Lokasenna 9), which is why the gods keep having to punish and forgive him. T2: he has two Asgard BROTHERS-BY-OATH mentioned in the sources: HELBLINDI and BYLEISTR (Gylfaginning 33) -- shadowy figures who never get their own stories, listed only to complete the giant genealogy. T3: by his ASGARD WIFE SIGYN he has two sons -- NARI (or NARFI) and VALI. These are the sons whose entrails will bind him in the cave (see punishment ladder). SIGYN'S NAME survives most famously in her single loyal image standing bowl-in-hand above her tortured husband. T4: by the GIANTESS ANGRBODA in Jotunheim he has three monstrous children -- FENRIR the wolf who will kill Odin at Ragnarok, JORMUNGANDR the world-serpent who will kill Thor at Ragnarok, and HEL the queen of the dead. That is one father-line making TWO of the three great Ragnarok-deaths of Aesir kings. T5: by the giant STALLION SVADILFARI -- with LOKI HIMSELF in mare-form -- he is the MOTHER of SLEIPNIR, the eight-legged horse ODIN rides. Snorri points out (Skaldskaparmal 23) that Loki is therefore 'kinsman' or 'father' of Sleipnir and Fenrir and Jormungandr and Hel and the sons Nari and Vali. In Lokasenna 33 Loki himself boasts of having born children as a mare and taunts other gods with sexual insults; the mare-birth is one of very few examples in world myth of a MALE deity giving birth. Further rungs: Loki's cross-tribe kinship is exactly why he keeps getting away with the tricks -- as sworn brother to Odin the gods can't just execute him for pranks; as father-of-monsters he keeps the story-engine of Norse myth turning; the phrase 'Loki's brood' becomes a Norse figure for a doomed line; some late-medieval Icelandic manuscripts try to gloss Loki as a devil-figure, but the ORIGINAL sources give him a family a wife a household a table and forgiveness right up to Baldr's death.
